DISARMING CITIZENS: SA, Lay Down Your Weapons

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This week Minister of Police Bheki Cele announced that South Africans should not own firearms. But crime is endemic to every day life in South Africa, is this the solution that will make already defen

Unique Selling Point:
In his announcement this week Minister Bheki Cele said that legislation was being looked at with regards to amending the Firearms Control Act. The Confederations of Hunting South Africa, says the amendments have been on the cards since 2011 and nothing has happened so far. They also say that limiting or removing a citizen’s rights to defend themselves has sinister overtones.

Summary:
South Africa is rated as 127th out of 163 countries as most violent. In many places the crime and murder rates outstrip some war zones. The amendments to the firearms control act, have far reaching repercussions, which include the security industry, Hunting licences the sporting sector, as well as individual rights.
Many South African’s rely on private security companies for safety, and their firearms quotas will also be limited under the proposed amendments, which means that an overburdened police service will be tasked with protecting ordinary people. A leaked version of the draft amended act was circulated, which government has denied is the final version and says it is one of many drafts. How will removing the rights of South African’s to own a weapon for self defence, curb crime? The amendment of the act does not tackle illegal firearms that are in circulation and used to commit many crimes. We challenge Minister Bheki Cele to consider the impact on South Africa’s spiral of crime when there is less armed defence against it.


Further information:
We speak to Martin Hood, a firearm law expert as well as Steven Palos from the Confederation of Hunting in South Africa, who are of the opinion that there is something far greater at stake in the long term, and that disarming individuals means more control for the state.

Steven Palos says that the current government has not engaged with the relevant stakeholders as yet, but they are hopeful that the portfolio committee will engage with them at some point, but he says that the Ministry of Police has shied away from any discourse, “for at least the past four years not one effort has been made by elements within Cele’s department to engage legitimate and accredited firearm stakeholder groups in this process. SAPS Legal, the Central Firearm Registry, the Civilian Secretariat for Police and the many police ministers and national commissioners have all singularly evaded their legal and civil responsibility to engage legitimate stakeholders at all, let alone in good faith”

His perspective is that Bheki Cele is waging war against law abiding citizens rather than the real perpetrators of crime. Statistically, arms that have been given in for example in the last amnesty phase, only 20% of them were found to be used in criminal activities.

Other parties like gun free SA will be contacted... this is a hotbed, as Gun Free SA feel very strongly that women who end up being victims of femicide is down to the ease of owning a firearm, and this of course is off the back of the high levels of crimes against women.

We need to secure an interview with Minister Bheki Cele to get his perspective on how these changes and specifically his aim to have no individuals owning firearms in the future, be a solution to the extreme violence facing South Africans daily.

Expert:
Mr. Martin Hood
Mr. Steve Palos
Mr. Bheki Cele Minister of Police
Mr. Gun Free South Africa.

Press Release:


Disarming Citizens
Police Minister Bheki Cele ideally wants South Africans not to own firearms. In a country rated as one of the most violent in the world; where crime and murder rates sometimes outstrip some war zones and where the safety of citizens is often in their own hands, Carte Blanche asks how it would impact the pervasive climate of crime in the country.
Producer: Sophia Phirippides| Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


LINK: South Africans are scared - living daily with the fear of murder, abuse and violent crimes. The Minister of Police Bheki Cele says ideally he would like to see a South Africa where individuals don’t own firearms,

Press Conference Bheki Cele: This firearms act which is under review, there is a noise about it again "one thing that we are trying to put there and will fight to put there - is that individuals should not have firearms"

LINK: Can removing guns from people make our world a safer place or is it part of a bigger societal problem?

VO: There are over 3 million legal firearms in South Africa, and the latest amnesty, which calls for citizens to hand in unlicensed and unwanted firearms, saw to date thousands of guns being surrendered to the police.

Sound up:
Press Conference Bheki Cele: "This could be the number of dead bodies."

VO: The Minister's words reignited the debate on gun ownership and its implications.

Martin: I don't think that any government minister says anything in isolation from what constitutes government policy, what he was doing was trying to sensitize the media and the public to the very fact that he's going to take away our firearms.

VO: Firearms Law Expert Martin Hood, red flagged the Minister's statements, as there has been no recent engagement from government with industry stakeholders,
a sentiment echoed by Gugu Bohali, vice chairperson of Gun Owners South Africa.

Gugu: The reason why it's taken us aback is the people who walk the streets, the everyday man, we are the ones suffering from the crime. you are saying we don't have the right to defend our lives.

VO: In an in-depth interview with Minister of Police Bheki Cele, we challenge the implications of his perspective on amendments to the Firearms Control Act that have been in the offing since 2015.

Cele: I would love to see the law saying individual and private citizens do not own firearms. It doesn't matter what Cele thinks and what Cele says. South Africans will have a say on that. But as we go on with the bill, with the amendment, that will be suggested from our side.

VO: The Minister considers countries like South Korea and Japan good role models, where individuals don't own firearms, and murder rates are minimal.

Cele: Their firearms belong to the armed forces either the police either, either the army and all that.

Masa: That would be noble minister, to have no guns in our society But is it fair to expect legal gun owners to give up their arms when there are so many illegal firearms in our system?

Cele: So it's nothing wrong having the noble idea that might not necessarily happen tomorrow but I'm not going to sit here and say that I wish to see our South Africans armed and forever armed and everybody has got a firearm.


VO: Firearms are the leading cause of murder in South Africa, and most gun related murders occur amongst people who are known to one another. Murder has increased by 35% over the last seven years.

On the other hand, hijackings, burglaries and robberies more often involve illegal firearms which are either smuggled into the country or were once legally owned.

Guy: Between about 1999 and 2015, we had about 140 000 licensed firearms that were lost or stolen .


VO: Doctor Guy Lamb, Director of the Safety and Violence Initiative at the University of Cape Town has been researching the role of firearms control and its impact on gun violence for over 8 years.

Guy: Most of the firearm crime in SA is committed with handguns. And most of those handguns would have been sourced either from civilian firearm owners or from the police.

Gugu: If someone comes to my house and murders me and takes my gun, you cannot start blaming the victim saying oh but he had a gun that's why he was murdered. if the policing was up to scratch they would catch criminals.

LINK: For many people owning a gun makes them feel more secure. Historically most of them are men but with unprecedented violence against females in South Africa it's become a growing trend amongst women to want to own a firearm for self-defense.

VO: Bianca Bell gave up her job as a real estate agent and became a firearms instructor, teaching women self defence after a traumatic home invasion.

Bianca and a friend had been out for dinner, and upon arriving back at her friend’s house they were confronted by an armed robber.

Bianca: We were held for about 45 minutes. After he'd robbed us of all of our valuables, //
Sound up Robber: Move Go to the Bedroom move…
Bianca: Then said he was going to rape us. I decided that it wasn't gonna happen and I fought back he shot at us twice. I managed to fight him off. Unfortunately in the process I had broken my back.
Masa: What made you decide that you know what I'm gonna get a firearm now?
Bianca: I'd been a reservist for 23 years and although we used firearms on duty, I'd never had a firearm of my own and that day made me realize that no one was going to protect us - We needed to do it ourselves.
Masa: And you don't fear that your own firearms will be used against you?
Bianca: That's the reason we do so much training it helps you prevent anyone from taking the firearm off you

VO: This is the first time Emmah Thinola is trying out a firearm. As a single mom who works long hours she feels the need to have some form of protection.

Masa: Are you considering getting your own firearm?

Emmah: Yes. I actually am. as a single mother, you get to be frightened. Most of the time it's not safe, especially If you're staying in a stand alone house. if you close your gate you need to watch who was coming behind you.

VO: According to Dr Lamb, the most vocal sectors of society aren't necessarily the only ones crying out for protection.

Guy: The areas with the highest crime rates are predominantly within the townships, are predominantly within informal settlements, those voices are saying we need a gun to protect ourselves. We're not hearing those voices.

VO: There is an argument that if people felt safer and protected by the police there would be no need to own firearms for self defence.

Guy: If you listen for example to community members and residents on the Cape flats The consistent comments coming out is we want the police and military to take the guns out of here, we want them to arrest the gangsters.

VO: In July 2019 Operation Lockdown was launched in the Cape Flats. Military and police joined forces in a major anti-crime offensive, in areas where murder rates often exceed those of war zones.

Guy: In Cape Town from about 2008 or 2009 is the murder rate starts to climb quite dramatically so from about 2010 to now, the murder rate doubles. from about 35, 36 per 100 000 to close to 70 per 100 000.


VO: These figures impacted the country’s murder rate as a whole. This localised spike, according to Dr Lamb, was in large part due to a syndicate within the police stealing 2400 confiscated weapons that were earmarked for destruction. They sold them on between 2007 and 2015 and they ended up in the hands of gangs in the Cape Flats and the Nelson Mandela Metropol. Many of these guns were later linked to 1066 murders.

Masa: What do you say to community members who don't have trust in the police?
Cele: There are many and they’re increasing, who say they do have trust in the police. I'll concede and agree with you that there are few of us as the members of the South African police that are bad apples that they give us a bad name.

VO: Minister Cele emphasises that the problem of crime is a societal issue. But shouldn’t effective policing encompass crime prevention?// In 2019 Carte Blanche covered the story of Samantha Wade who was shot by her ex-fiance and left for dead. Miraculously, she survived, but he went on to kill himself. This tragedy may have been prevented had police acted on Samantha's pleas the night before.

Sound Up: Samantha: The commander of the police station said this is a domestic dispute by tomorrow it will be over, and we were begging him please go there and confiscate the guns.

Martin: If the police get a report of domestic violence, they should take away dangerous objects. That doesn't happen. And that points not towards a problem with a firearm but towards a problem with policing.

Link: Civilian Firearms are used in many sectors in society which include hunting, sport and the private security industry. These could be severely affected should amendments to legislation become too prohibitive or restrictive.

Cele: So it will be fine if the guns are reduced even for those that are going for sports, are going for hunting sports but definitely the law will take that one on board.

Martin: It imposes restrictions on the number of firearms, the type of firearms that can be licensed by people that are sport shooters or hunters.

Cele: If you are a hunter you have eight guns, why should you have 80 guns, we can't have the country that every house is an armoury.

VO: Similarly the Minister is adamant that stricter regulations need to be placed on the private security industry.

Cele: We can't have private security that is more armed, is more powerful. You know South African police if I'm not mistaken we’re about 197 000 in the country. Private security is 216 000, Gauteng alone.

Masa: So where are we in this process?
Cele: I hope to take it to cabinet the first part of this year. We will draft what we think is best for South Africans and South Africans will decide what is best for them.*

Most of the time it's not safe, especially If you're staying in a stand alone house. if you close your gate you need to watch who was coming behind you. VO: According to Dr Lamb, the most vocal sectors of society aren't necessarily the only ones crying out for protection. Guy: The areas with the highest crime rates are predominantly within the townships, are predominantly within informal settlements, those voices are saying we need a gun to protect ourselves. We're not hearing those voices. VO: There is an argument that if people felt safer and protected by the police there would be no need to own firearms for self defence. Guy: If you listen for example to community members and residents on the Cape flats The consistent comments coming out is we want the police and military to take the guns out of here, we want them to arrest the gangsters. VO: In July 2019 Operation Lockdown was launched in the Cape Flats. Military and police joined forces in a major anti-crime offensive, in areas where murder rates often exceed those of war zones. Guy: In Cape Town from about 2008 or 2009 is the murder rate starts to climb quite dramatically so from about 2010 to now, the murder rate doubles. from about 35, 36 per 100 000 to close to 70 per 100 000. VO: These figures impacted the country’s murder rate as a whole. This localised spike, according to Dr Lamb, was in large part due to a syndicate within the police stealing 2400 confiscated weapons that were earmarked for destruction. They sold them on between 2007 and 2015 and they ended up in the hands of gangs in the Cape Flats and the Nelson Mandela Metropol. Many of these guns were later linked to 1066 murders. Masa: What do you say to community members who don't have trust in the police? Cele: There are many and they’re increasing, who say they do have trust in the police. I'll concede and agree with you that there are few of us as the members of the South African police that are bad apples that they give us a bad name. VO: Minister Cele emphasises that the problem of crime is a societal issue. But shouldn’t effective policing encompass crime prevention?// In 2019 Carte Blanche covered the story of Samantha Wade who was shot by her ex-fiance and left for dead. Miraculously, she survived, but he went on to kill himself. This tragedy may have been prevented had police acted on Samantha's pleas the night before. Sound Up: Samantha: The commander of the police station said this is a domestic dispute by tomorrow it will be over, and we were begging him please go there and confiscate the guns. Martin: If the police get a report of domestic violence, they should take away dangerous objects. That doesn't happen. And that points not towards a problem with a firearm but towards a problem with policing. Link: Civilian Firearms are used in many sectors in society which include hunting, sport and the private security industry. These could be severely affected should amendments to legislation become too prohibitive or restrictive. Cele: So it will be fine if the guns are reduced even for those that are going for sports, are going for hunting sports but definitely the law will take that one on board. Martin: It imposes restrictions on the number of firearms, the type of firearms that can be licensed by people that are sport shooters or hunters. Cele: If you are a hunter you have eight guns, why should you have 80 guns, we can't have the country that every house is an armoury. VO: Similarly the Minister is adamant that stricter regulations need to be placed on the private security industry. Cele: We can't have private security that is more armed, is more powerful. You know South African police if I'm not mistaken we’re about 197 000 in the country. Private security is 216 000, Gauteng alone. Masa: So where are we in this process? Cele: I hope to take it to cabinet the first part of this year. We will draft what we think is best for South Africans and South Africans will decide what is best for them.*

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): This week Minister of Police Bheki Cele announced that South Africans should not own firearms. But crime is endemic to every day life in South Africa, is this the solution that will make already defen
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In his announcement this week Minister Bheki Cele said that legislation was being looked at with regards to amending the Firearms Control Act. The Confederations of Hunting South Africa, says the amendments have been on the cards since 2011 and nothing has happened so far. They also say that limiting or removing a citizen’s rights to defend themselves has sinister overtones.
metadata.Summary: South Africa is rated as 127th out of 163 countries as most violent. In many places the crime and murder rates outstrip some war zones. The amendments to the firearms control act, have far reaching repercussions, which include the security industry, Hunting licences the sporting sector, as well as individual rights. Many South African’s rely on private security companies for safety, and their firearms quotas will also be limited under the proposed amendments, which means that an overburdened police service will be tasked with protecting ordinary people. A leaked version of the draft amended act was circulated, which government has denied is the final version and says it is one of many drafts. How will removing the rights of South African’s to own a weapon for self defence, curb crime? The amendment of the act does not tackle illegal firearms that are in circulation and used to commit many crimes. We challenge Minister Bheki Cele to consider the impact on South Africa’s spiral of crime when there is less armed defence against it.
metadata.Further information: We speak to Martin Hood, a firearm law expert as well as Steven Palos from the Confederation of Hunting in South Africa, who are of the opinion that there is something far greater at stake in the long term, and that disarming individuals means more control for the state. Steven Palos says that the current government has not engaged with the relevant stakeholders as yet, but they are hopeful that the portfolio committee will engage with them at some point, but he says that the Ministry of Police has shied away from any discourse, “for at least the past four years not one effort has been made by elements within Cele’s department to engage legitimate and accredited firearm stakeholder groups in this process. SAPS Legal, the Central Firearm Registry, the Civilian Secretariat for Police and the many police ministers and national commissioners have all singularly evaded their legal and civil responsibility to engage legitimate stakeholders at all, let alone in good faith” His perspective is that Bheki Cele is waging war against law abiding citizens rather than the real perpetrators of crime. Statistically, arms that have been given in for example in the last amnesty phase, only 20% of them were found to be used in criminal activities. Other parties like gun free SA will be contacted... this is a hotbed, as Gun Free SA feel very strongly that women who end up being victims of femicide is down to the ease of owning a firearm, and this of course is off the back of the high levels of crimes against women. We need to secure an interview with Minister Bheki Cele to get his perspective on how these changes and specifically his aim to have no individuals owning firearms in the future, be a solution to the extreme violence facing South Africans daily.
